notes: Tagged repository baseline euro-2028-baseline remains contract 63. Contracts 64–100 establish the multi-competition season foundations, domestic game engines, Cup-neutral sources, provider custody and the two tournament-path corrections. Contract 101 removes obsolete shared-league gating from Euro post-lock reveal without widening pre-lock access. Contract 102 persists the Predictor Championship split as a distinct phase. Contract 103 reconciles game availability with repeatable competition instances: one live public row per season game, one live row per independent series, public/private coexistence, scoped predecessor lineage and bounded completion reasons. Contract 104 keeps five operational callers live-only and moves five read surfaces onto a current-public resolver that prefers live and otherwise retains the latest terminal result; Contract 102 Cup phase filters remain intact. Contract 105 enforces one-parent split ancestry and derives the continuing Championship table from settled initial and split fixtures without copying a starting total. Contract 107 is the Last Man Standing restart itself: it completes a wiped-out competition as no_winner_restarted, creates one linked successor, re-enters every entrant and copies no selections, cycles, projections or windows. Contract 108 guards the gap that deferral leaves — a successor may not hold a round that opened or locked before its predecessor finished, so the catalogue publisher cannot give a fresh competition rounds nobody could play in. Contract 109 closes the deferral itself: the next eligible league round is derived from the existing matchweek lock authority, the successor's calendar is generated from it exactly once, and an hourly job drives the restart from what settlement reported. Settlement continues only to derive and report. Contract 110 gives the season Predictor Championship rounds it can be played over: until it, nothing in the repository created a window for a season competition while bonus_cup_fixtures.window_id is NOT NULL, so no season Championship fixture could be persisted in either phase. It schedules N rounds from the next eligible league matchweeks, refuses a season that cannot supply the whole format rather than truncating it, and appends rather than owning the calendar so the split phase can be scheduled on the same competition later. Contract 111 launches a season Championship: threshold, format, initial group, draw, rounds and round-robin fixtures. It drives the single-group shape and refuses the multi-group one by name. The public threshold applies only to public competitions — a hundred-entrant field always takes the multi-group shape, so the shape this drives belongs to organiser-created private competitions. Hosted deployment remains separately guarded and is not claimed by this repository contract. Contract 114 gives the season matchweek card its bounded browser path: one read and three writes scoped to the caller's own entry, with locks, the Joker allowance and version conflicts enforced by the triggers that already own them, a version column and PT409 trigger on season_predictions, and the delete path brought under the matchweek lock so clearing a prediction or taking back a Joker after lock refuses. No table grant is added and no rule moves. Contract 115 makes the database able to call out at all: it installs pg_net, forbids any browser-reachable function in an exposed schema from calling into net, and drives the deployed provider-poll Edge Function from pg_cron at the cadence each target declares. pg_net's own grants belong to whoever owns the extension — where Supabase's image owns it, postgres is neither superuser nor a member of supabase_admin and cannot revoke them, which CI established by refusing the first version of the migration rather than by review. It records no poll target and imports no fixture, so on application the job runs and does nothing. Contract 116 lets a season Last Man Standing entrant SEE the round they can already pick in: contract 86 widened the selection trigger to season fixtures but the READ was never widened, so get_my_lms resolves every window through bonus_window_fixtures joined to public.matches and returns a season round with an empty fixture array. get_season_lms_round reads season_cup_window_fixtures joined to season_fixtures instead, and returns the survival verdict from predictor_internal.season_lms_pick_outcome — the same authority the settlement replay folds over — rather than handing a browser raw scores to judge, because a season fixture carries no winner column. It returns one round, the earliest still open to a pick, and nothing about any other entrant. No table grant is added and no rule moves. Contract 117 is the repeatable path a provider kickoff change takes to the fixture: it revises an existing kickoff, creates none, deletes none and never writes competition_round_id, which is the owner amendment made executable. It fails closed on the whole payload when any identifier is unmapped, refuses a kickoff moved into the past and a fixture no longer scheduled, and records every move append-only as an administrator review queue. Contract 118 stops the games hub being blind to a season's fixtures: get_bonus_games built its per-window fixtures from bonus_window_fixtures joined to public.matches with no branch on competition kind, so a season window returned an empty array — and because resolveCompetitionStatus can only settle a window when total > 0 and confirmed >= total, a season competition's first locked round stayed in flight permanently and the hub card stuck on it. Three internal functions supply the facts instead: a tournament limb, a season limb mapping season status onto the tournament vocabulary on contract 77's established equivalence, and a neutral combiner that unions rather than branches because a window's fixtures live in exactly one source. get_bonus_games is redefined from contract 104's text with only its fixtures subquery changed, verified by diff rather than by reading. This is the fourth instance of one defect — contracts 86, 98, 116 and this — and 168_tournament_only_browser_reads.sql now catches the fifth; get_bonus_games leaves that list by earning its removal. No table grant is added, no browser function is added, and no rule moves. Contract 119 makes a rescheduled fixture lock at its own kickoff. Contract 117 let a provider move a kickoff automatically and the lock did not follow, so a fixture postponed to the following Wednesday still locked on Saturday. Only a rescheduled fixture is affected — the owner chose that reading over the universal per-fixture one, which shares the same arithmetic but would make an ordinary matchweek predictable in stages. "Moved" is contract 117's revision record, a stored fact rather than an inference, and the rule is strictly permissive: it can extend an editing window, never shorten one. Contract 120 gives the Predictor Championship's phase and continuing table a bounded browser read. Contract 102 persists the split as a distinct phase and contract 105 derives its continuing table, and no browser-reachable function read either — measured on hosted development, zero functions authenticated may execute read cup_split_group_tables, parent_group_id or cup_final_group_tables, and get_my_cup was last defined on 29 July 2026, before the split phase existed. Fifth instance of the contract 86/98/116/118 defect, along the initial-versus-split axis rather than the tournament-versus-season one. get_season_cup_phase returns the caller's own phase and their own group's table from whichever authority owns that phase: cup_split_group_tables already filters phase_kind = 'split', so the branch is a lookup of an established fact rather than a new decision. It adds no rule, recomputes nothing, joins no profile, and gives a non-entrant entered=false rather than an exception. Contract 121 gives a season's play context: which season a URL means, and which matchweek its card opens at. Registering the UI-04 surface needed two facts the browser cannot obtain. The slug lives in public.competitions, which is revoked from every browser role and returned by no function, and two seasons sharing a season_key are told apart only by competition_id — the column pointing at the table the browser cannot read; (competitions.slug, tournaments.season_key) is a real composite key because both are unique. Contract 114's read then takes the matchweek as an argument and nothing told the caller what to pass; public.competition_rounds is revoked from the browser, so a client cannot derive it either, and deriving it in JavaScript would put a second answer beside the one the database owns. Nothing new is decided: predictor_internal.next_eligible_league_round already answers this for the Last Man Standing successor scheduler, ordering by the DERIVED lock instant rather than by ordinal so a rescheduled season resolves to the round that actually locks next — the property contract 119 made matter. This exposes that answer and adds no scheduling logic. It returns no prediction, entry, standing or other player, so it is not gated on an entry; a season past its last lock reports a null matchweek as an ordinary end-of-season state, while an unknown competition or a tournament-shaped one raises, because a single null for both would let a typo read as a finished season. No table grant is added and no rule moves. Contract 122 makes the two retention tables ADR 0012 names answerable at last: monthlyStandings and rollingFormPoints have existed in src/domain/season/standings.ts since contract 94 and were called by nothing. Both are derived views over settled matchweek totals and neither writes a score, a standing or a settlement — the cumulative total remains the only ranking that decides a season. A matchweek belongs to exactly one month because season_matchweek_scores is keyed per matchweek and never per fixture, so the only question is which instant names it: the round's window_opens_at, read in the competition's own display_timezone, because a month boundary is not a UTC fact and a 23:30Z kickoff on 31 July is August in Europe/London. An unplaceable settled matchweek refuses the whole monthly table rather than misranking a month, mirroring the TypeScript's null. Form needs no calendar at all — most-recent is an order, and competition_rounds.ordinal already carries it — so it answers on a season whose windows were never derived. The migration also runs contract 113's derive_round_play_windows once per league season, which nothing had ever called, leaving every window null. Keeping them fresh is deliberately NOT added: exactly one function moves a season kickoff, contract 117's provider import, and re-deriving after it could make an ordinary import start failing when a postponed fixture extends a round's span into the next round's, which contract 113's disjointness trigger refuses. That is a behaviour change to ingestion rather than to a standings view, so it stays an owner decision. Contract 123 refreshes a round play window that a provider revision made stale, and queues a conflicting refresh rather than failing the import. Contract 113 derives a round's play span from its own fixtures' kickoffs and STORES it; contract 117 moves those kickoffs automatically; nothing has ever run between the two, so from the first provider revision the stored window describes a kickoff that no longer exists. Contract 122 found this and deliberately left it, because the obvious driver carries a consequence: a postponed fixture EXTENDS its round's span, contract 113's disjointness trigger refuses two rounds claiming one instant, and automatic re-derivation could therefore make an ordinary provider import start failing. The refresh is built so that it cannot. It is per round rather than per season, it walks the target rounds in ordinal order against the calendar as it stands, and on an overlap it NEVER raises: the old window stays exactly as it is and the proposal is recorded append-only with the window it would have replaced, the round that blocked it and that round's window at the time. The three alternatives are refused for stated reasons — raising fails a whole season's import over one postponed fixture, applying anyway is the ambiguity contract 113 exists to exclude, and widening the blocking round invents contract 113's TILED reading inside an automatic ingestion path. One open row per round per proposal, so contract 115's hourly poll cannot fill the queue with copies of one unresolved conflict, while a further reschedule proposing a different span earns its own row. Ordering decides the outcome and never the correctness: a round refused against a neighbour that moves later in the same pass is deferred, and the next run applies it with nobody resolving anything by hand. Contract 117's importer is redefined from its own committed text with one change — it collects the rounds whose fixtures it moved and refreshes those windows inside the same transaction — verified by diff rather than by reading, and it still never writes competition_round_id, so the owner amendment is untouched. The exposure closed is bounded and stated rather than inflated: the only live consumer of the stored window is contract 122's month calendar, which reads window_opens_at alone, so a stale window misfiles a matchweek into the wrong monthly table and does nothing else. No browser-reachable function is added, no table grant is added, no lock, score, prediction, standing or settlement is written, and the migration applies with the queue empty. Contract 124 makes the Predictor Championship split actually happen. Contract 102 persists the split phase, contract 105 derives the continuing table and contract 120 gives it a browser read, and nothing had ever written a split-phase row — so cup_split_group_tables had never returned one and get_season_cup_phase's split branch was unreachable from any state this database could reach. src/domain/season/cupGroupTable.ts had the same shape on the other side: executeCupSplit is exported, tested and called by nothing. Same authority-with-no-caller pattern as contracts 116, 118, 120 and 122. The plan comes from contract 111's championship_launched audit record rather than from re-running select_season_cup_format, because that function answers 'what fits in the rounds that are LEFT' and the league phase has since been played; the arithmetic is still checked against the stored plan, and a disagreement refuses rather than picking one. The larger half goes to the top, which executeCupSplit and the format selector already both compute as the ceiling, so thirteen becomes seven and six. ADR 0014's stated-behaviour loose end is closed: both halves play in the same windows and the smaller half simply has no fixture in the last round or two, because matchday is the COMPETITION's round number and giving each half its own window run would make round 36 mean two different weeks depending on which half you are in. Draw numbers are carried rather than reassigned, since they terminate the tie-break sequence. Nobody is eliminated. Idempotent under an advisory lock. A multi-group field raises, because ADR 0014 is explicit that merging top halves across groups would carry points earned against different opponents; not-launched, no-split-in-format and an unsettled initial phase are ordinary outcomes a scheduled caller retries. It also fixes a latent defect it would otherwise have lit: cup_final_group_tables built its members CTE with no phase filter and grouped window totals by user_id alone, so an entrant holding both an initial and a split membership had their sequence 1-3 window totals summed twice. The filter is added in the same migration that makes it reachable and is behaviour-neutral to every existing row. No browser-reachable function is added, no table grant is added, and the migration creates no split group on application. Contract 125 lets a season fixture be given a result, which nothing in this repository could do. Measured: no migration anywhere writes season_fixtures.home_score or away_score; the only statement that writes that table at all is contract 117's importer, which sets kickoff_at and nothing else; and the three admin result RPCs operate on public.matches, the tournament shape, while a season's points live in season_matchweek_scores and never reach matches. Every season surface downstream of a result was therefore honest and empty — no matchweek settled, the leaderboard had nothing to rank, contract 122's monthly and rolling-form tables had no settled matchweek to place, and the Matches surface showed every fixture blank. It writes a result and records that it did, and settles nothing: process_due_season_matchweek_scores already rederives every league season on every run with no already-scored filter, precisely so a correction is picked up without its writer knowing anything about scoring. The protected confirmation gate holds by construction rather than by a new mechanism — after this contract exactly four functions write season_fixtures and only the three admin entry points can write a score, which the parity guard asserts across every migration rather than across this one. The gate is predictor_internal.require_result_admin(), the same authority the tournament path uses, reused rather than reimplemented. The signature carries one pair of scores and no method, extra time or penalties, because a league fixture is ninety minutes and may be drawn; that is ADR 0012's rule rather than an omission. A reason is required to correct or clear and not to confirm — deliberately stricter than the tournament path, because by the time a season result is corrected points have been banked against it. Revisions are numbered per fixture, carry the result they replaced and the actor, and may be neither updated nor deleted: unlike contracts 117 and 123 there is no reviewed flag, so a mistake is corrected by recording another revision. The revision record is internal and unread by any browser, deliberately: contract 117's revision queue and contract 123's refresh-conflict queue are unread too, and one administrator surface should read all three rather than this contract inventing a third shape. Fixture lifecycle is not owned here — nothing moves a fixture into postponed, abandoned or void, though a postponed fixture eventually played is accepted as the ordinary case. Contract 126 lets a game that has not started be rejoined, which the deploy preview found: leaving the season Last Man Standing competition refused re-entry on a competition where bonus_competition_windows held zero rows for all six season games — no round existed, none had opened or locked, no club had been picked and nothing had settled. last_man_standing is the only game_definitions row with allow_rejoin false, and join_competition_game read that flag alone, so the refusal was permanent from publication, months before the game can be played. This enforces the rule rather than changing it. ADR 0013 says entry closes after round one and the field is fixed once the first round locks; ADR 0020 says leaving never permits rejoining that same RUNNING competition, consistent with the rolling-entry rejection — whose own stated reason is depletion, a player joining at round eight arriving with all twenty clubs while survivors have burned eight. Before the first lock that asymmetry does not exist. Running is the first window whose locks_at has passed: ADR 0013's own boundary and the instant its other rules already turn on. Not first window created, because a calendar published weeks ahead has fixed nothing; not first pick saved, because one entrant's selection would close entry for everybody and make the boundary depend on another player's behaviour. game_definitions is not touched, so which games refuse is unchanged and the behaviour change reaches exactly one game. The disqualification, duplicate-entry, availability and registration refusals all sit above this one and are asserted to have survived the redefinition, which is verified by diff against the committed text rather than by reading. Nothing survives a leave to be inherited on rejoin: leave_competition_game deletes the bonus_competition_entrants row and season_lms_entrant_state cascades off it. Contract 127 lets a season competition be opened for play at all. Measured on hosted development rather than inferred: two league seasons published with a full fixture list, every kickoff set and every round play window derived, six competitions published and active with entrants already joined, and not one of them playable. Both season Last Man Standing competitions hold zero rounds and no season_lms_setups row, so settle_season_lms_competition answers refused/no_setup; both season Championships hold zero groups, because contract 111's launch driver has never had a caller. Same authority-with-no-caller shape as contracts 116, 118, 120, 122 and 124, at the acquisition end. The bootstrap is an OPERATOR ACTION and not a job, which is the decision contract 122 left open: launch_season_cup fixes the format, the draw and the whole fixture list at whatever field size it finds and refuses ever after, so a cron tick would be choosing the competition's shape, and a Last Man Standing calendar is the same in kind — created once and never rescheduled, because rescheduling moves locks under selections already made. Everything is idempotent and takes its boundary as an argument, so turning it into a driver later remains available and is a separate decision. A first instance needs its own generator because contract 109 refuses one by name, and the catalogue it defers to is scripts/bonus-games/publish-catalogue.sql, which publishes the Euro 2028 tournament's fixed seven-round plan and only that; a league season has no catalogue and never will, since its rounds come from its own fixture list. The two generators stay non-competing by refusing each other's case rather than sharing a boundary, and their derivation is asserted character-identical after normalising the one thing that legitimately differs — what the calendar starts after — because a drift would let two competitions in one season lock the same matchweek at different instants and neither pgTAP suite would notice. Main Predictor is deliberately given nothing: its rounds ARE the season's matchweeks and its lock derives from season_fixtures.kickoff_at every time, so a window here would be a second source for the same lock; the dispatch reports that in an outcome rather than staying silent, because 'nothing to do' and 'not handled' are otherwise indistinguishable to a caller. A PRIVATE Last Man Standing competition is refused rather than given Classic, since ADR 0013 makes those rules its organiser's; only the public setup is written, and only because ADR 0022 pins it to Classic and season_lms_setups_public_is_classic would refuse any other public row. The gate is a new predictor_internal.require_competition_admin() rather than require_result_admin: both admit super_admin, and an account trusted to correct a scoreline has not thereby been trusted to fix a season's draw. Nothing here settles, scores or completes anything — results still arrive through the protected confirmation gate and the existing rederivation jobs do the rest — and the migration opens no competition on application. Contract 128 gives a season league a standings table of its own, because the one it had was the tournament's. get_league_members reads predictor_internal.standing_metrics (score_events, matches, match_predictions) and derives its final-tie-break switch from public.matches — none of which a competition season writes, since its points are banked per matchweek in season_matchweek_scores. Measured on hosted development: the two league seasons hold 0 rows in score_events and 0 in matches against 380 and 198 season_fixtures, so a league on a season returned EVERY MEMBER ON ZERO, ranked alphabetically, with no error. Leagues have been season-capable since contract 66 gave public.leagues a game_competition_id and backfilled a league season to its main_predictor availability, and create_game_league accepts any game competition — so this was a surface that answered wrongly rather than one that did not exist. Sixth instance of the contract 86/98/116/118/120 shape. It is a NEW read rather than a widened one, unlike contract 118's get_bonus_games, because the two kinds do not answer the same question: the tournament table carries exact scores, correct outcomes, correct knockout teams, the champion and a group-goals tie-break, and ADR 0012 ranks a season on cumulative points alone while pairing the total with matchweeks played. Points and matchweeks played come from predictor_internal.season_standings, the same authority get_season_leaderboard reads, so a league total cannot disagree with the season total for the same player; the RANK is recomputed inside the league, because a private league is its own table and its leader is its best member rather than 47th in the season. A member with no entry is listed on zero rather than omitted, matching both get_league_members and season_standings' own LEFT join. get_league_members is redefined from its own committed text with ONE guard inserted — verified by diff — and now REFUSES a season league by naming the read that answers, because adding the season read while leaving the wrong one reachable for the same league is half a fix and a fabricated all-zero table looks like a real answer. No score, settlement or standing is written; both functions are reads and the migration asserts they are declared stable. Contract 129 gives a season a head-to-head at all: get_rival_entry reads entries.submitted_at, entry_totals, match_predictions over public.matches and predicted_progression, none of which a competition season writes, so there was no comparison rather than a wrong one. The reveal boundary is the difference that matters — the tournament compares against one instant, tournaments.lock_at, and a season locks per matchweek, so the boundary is predictor_internal.season_matchweek_lock_at, the same derivation the write trigger enforces. One deliberate asymmetry, in the safe direction: that function returns null when a round's kickoffs are incomplete and the write trigger calls that LOCKED, while this calls it NOT REVEALED — the picks are final either way, and revealing on a null would expose a season whose kickoffs were never published. Who may look is contract 95's rule, both players holding an entry, deliberately not get_rival_entry's shared-league rule, because the season leaderboard already shows every entrant to every entrant; narrowing it later remains available and widening it afterwards would not. Both sides of the comparison are built by one internal function called twice, so a copied block cannot diverge and show the caller their own Joker beside their opponent's points. Contract 130 then adds the season prediction consensus, KEYED ON THE ROUND rather than the season for the same reason: the tournament's is a single answer for a single lock, and a season has no such instant. The minimum cohort is contract 61's ten, reused rather than re-decided, but what it counts is the entries that predicted THAT MATCHWEEK — a season with fifty entrants of whom six played matchweek 30 is exactly the case the protection exists for, and a season-wide count would report it as safe. Suppression returns rather than raises, matching the tournament shape, and the read names no individual: counts per scoreline, bounded at five, and no join to profiles at all, asserted on application. Contract 131 then makes the retention tables able to name their players, OPTIONALLY and off by default, so contract 122's decision to return entry_id alone is preserved as the default rather than overturned: a caller that already holds the names asks for exactly what 122 returned, and a surface with no leaderboard beside it can ask for them instead of rendering every opponent as Entrant. There is ONE reachable signature, with a REQUIRED fourth parameter, and the route was arrived at by elimination against guards this repository already has: a DEFAULTED fourth parameter overloads rather than replaces and makes a three-argument call ambiguous; DROPPING the three-argument form is destructive at migration level and the additive checker refuses it, correctly, since one optional display name is not a reason to put a batch through the backup-and-rehearsal rollout; and KEEPING BOTH arities needs both granted, which rpcAllowlistParity requires to be declared while the contract validator refuses two entries of the same name. So the three-argument function is left in the catalogue and REVOKED — additive, and no second body of the same read stays reachable — and its one caller, src/services/supabase/seasonPeriodStandings.ts, moves in the same change with the flag defaulted to false there. The naming is a mapping over what the authorities returned, preserving array order, so season_monthly_standings and season_form_standings keep their parity with src/domain/season/standings.ts and neither reads a profile. Contract 132 replaces the one-off initial domestic fixture adoption gap with an auditable proposal boundary: contract-132 normalized provider evidence can be staged without publishing anything, and a competition administrator may approve only a complete initial Scottish Premiership (198/33/12) or Premier League (380/38/20) calendar. Approval creates scheduled fixtures, clubs, matchweeks and provider mappings while retaining provider status/scores as evidence only; official results still require the protected result authority. Contract 133 exposes caller-owned season Predictor Championship instances and one explicit player view without granting private Cup tables: private discovery requires existing entrant membership, direct private-id probing by an outsider is indistinguishable from a missing id, the phase/table remains owned by get_season_cup_phase, and fixture scores/settlement remain owned by the existing neutral Cup authorities. Contract 134 removes the browser privileges Supabase's default grants left on public.rate_limit_events, the one server-only table in this repository whose creating migration declared "no client access at all" and then revoked nothing: anon and authenticated held select, insert, update, delete, truncate, references and trigger on a limiter log protected only by a policy-less row-level security. It revokes the table and its identity sequence from both browser roles, leaves service_role, row-level security, the thresholds, the enforcement function and both triggers untouched, and proves in pgTAP that the definer function still writes, still refuses at its ceiling and still prunes. Contract 135 implements the owner decision of 9 August 2026 amending ADR 0020: a provider result becomes the official season result without a human typing it, and it stays auditable and correctable. It supplies the status vocabulary a result is decided by, the provisional live projection, the provenance and refusal records, and the scheduled driver that finally calls contracts 117 and 132 — both of which had no caller anywhere in the repository. A provider write reaches season_fixtures only through contract 125's audited writer, and an administrator's correction stops the provider writing that fixture again. The tournament path is untouched. Contract 136 gives a club a code and colours, resolved at read time from an owner-controlled reference, so ClubIdentity stops rendering every club as the same blank shirt; it adds no column to public.teams and no browser-reachable relation. Contract 137 corrects a defect contract 136 shipped: the club name normaliser stripped the alternation (afc|fc) from the end of a name whose spaces had already been removed, so 'Chelsea FC' normalised to 'chelse' and 'Aston Villa FC' to 'astonvill', and both rendered in the neutral fallback. The tokens are now removed as whole words before the spaces go. Found by verifying the hosted development rollout against real football rather than against the migration ledger: 29 of 32 clubs resolved, and the three that did not were the only evidence anything was wrong. Contract 138 gives an administrator the review queues nothing could see: measured, seven append-only queues existed and the only browser-reachable functions naming any of them were contract 132's two decision writers. It reads all of them bounded per section and lets an administrator acknowledge an item, which contracts 117 and 123 had always anticipated with a reviewed_at nothing ever set. Acknowledging is never a decision about the item. Contract 139 gives a season a fixtures read at all, ordered by kickoff and labelled by round, which closes the ADR 0020 amendment item that had no implementation because a season had no fixture list: a match postponed out of matchweek 5 into November now sorts into November while still saying Matchweek 5. Contract 140 gives a Leave control the fact it needs to predict itself: leave_competition_game refuses once a bonus_score_events row exists for the caller and nothing exposed that, so the dashboard could only render a control the server would refuse or hide one that would have worked. Contract 141 derives recent club form and club head-to-head from settled season fixtures alone, which the enrichment plan classes as derive-ourselves work and which contract 135 made possible by producing results at all; it reads no prediction, entry or score event. Contract 142 maps SportMonks state 22 to in play, measured from retained payloads rather than documentation: the same fixture carried that token with a different score at different times, and a score cannot change after full time. It writes no result and settles nothing; it fixes the live projection for a fixture observed during its second half. It is the first thing contract 135's fail-closed vocabulary and contract 138's review queue found together. Contract 145 closes the atomicity half of risk-register DATA-007: enforce_rate_limit counted, compared and then inserted with nothing between the read and the write, so under read-committed isolation N concurrent transactions for one caller each saw a count below the ceiling and all proceeded. It now takes a transaction-scoped advisory lock keyed on the caller before the prune, the count and the insert, which is the idiom 20260727191942_operating_cap_enforcement.sql already uses for the two site-wide counters. One key per caller and never per action, so the function cannot hold two of its own locks and cannot deadlock against itself. No relation, policy, trigger, threshold, grant or rule moves, and the ceilings stay at their original call sites so the TypeScript/PostgreSQL parity check compares the same two sides. It does not close the rest of DATA-007 — invalid operations still consume no limit, the expensive read RPCs are still unbounded, and there are still no edge/IP controls or alerting. Contract 159 closes the half of SEC-001 that contract 158 left open on a second door: public.resolve_invite_code was recreated by 158 to widen its shape check and carried neither of that contract’s two fixes, so the universal code entry point charged no limiter at all and returned the target id, the member count and, for a private competition, an ownership flag — a wider and cheaper confirmation oracle than the get_league_preview SEC-001 forced narrowed. It now charges the same league_invite_probe action at the same ceiling before the shape check and before the lookup, so all three doors draw on one budget, and it no longer returns an id or a member count for either container kind. Contract 160 closes MIG-UI-13, the competition’s own league table: per-season points values, an ordered tie-break vocabulary applied server-side including a head-to-head mini-league computed among the clubs actually tied, promotion/playoff/relegation boundaries counted against the real field size, signed points adjustments that apply only from effective_from, and awarded outcomes stored beside a fixture rather than in it — because season_fixtures.home_score is what predictions were settled against, and writing an award there would rescore a settled matchweek months later. get_competition_table is granted to authenticated only and refuses any competition that is not a league season, so it cannot become a discovery surface for Euro 2028. Contract 169 adds no browser-reachable signature: it corrects the SPAN a season Predictor Championship group table is ranked over. predictor_internal.cup_season_group_tables measures every ADR 0014 key over the windows of the entrant’s own settled group fixtures rather than over the tournament’s three matchdays, cup_initial_group_tables is the single dispatcher both season reads now call, and cup_final_group_tables is deliberately untouched because it is the tournament’s production-hosted authority. get_season_cup_phase gains one key, table_source, naming which authority ranked the table. Contract 170 adds the action centre’s matchweek generator and adds no browser-reachable signature: process_player_action_items keeps its name, its service_role-only grant and its shape, gaining one more counter.
